prompt: The 'rate of a reaction' means…
options: the total amount of product that can be made
how fast the reactants are used up (or products formed)
whether the reaction gives out heat
the temperature of the reaction mixture
explanation: Rate is about speed — how quickly reactants turn into products.
hint: Rate = speed: is the reaction fast or slow?

prompt: According to collision theory, a chemical reaction happens when particles…
options: collide with enough energy and a suitable orientation
explanation: Particles must collide hard enough (at least the activation energy) and lined up the right way for a reaction to occur.
hint: Particles have to bump into each other — hard enough, and the right way round.

prompt: Which of these would speed up a reaction?
options: increasing the concentration of a reactant
using larger lumps of solid instead of powder
explanation: Higher concentration → particles more crowded → more collisions per second → faster reaction.
hint: Which change makes the reacting particles collide more often?

prompt: Increasing the temperature speeds up a reaction mainly because the particles…
options: move faster, so they collide more often and with more energy
explanation: Heat gives particles more kinetic energy: collisions become more frequent AND a bigger fraction of them have enough energy to react.
hint: Hot particles move faster — what does that do to their collisions?

prompt: Powdered marble reacts with acid faster than a single marble chip of the same mass because the powder has…
options: a larger surface area exposed to the acid
explanation: Breaking a solid into smaller pieces exposes far more surface, so more acid particles can collide with it at once.
hint: Crushing a solid increases what — the surface that's exposed.

prompt: A catalyst is a substance that…
options: is used up during the reaction
speeds up a reaction without being used up
explanation: A catalyst speeds a reaction by lowering the activation energy, and it can be recovered unchanged afterwards.
hint: It helps the reaction along but doesn't get consumed.

prompt: Enzymes are best described as…
explanation: Enzymes are catalysts made by living things — they speed up the reactions inside organisms.
hint: They're catalysts found in living things.

prompt: On a graph of 'volume of gas produced' against 'time', a STEEPER line means the reaction is…
explanation: A steeper gradient = more gas made per second = a faster rate.
hint: Steep slope = lots happening quickly.

prompt: On a graph of 'volume of gas produced' against 'time', the line flattens out (goes horizontal) when…
options: a reactant has run out, so the reaction has finished
explanation: When no more gas is being made, a reactant must be used up — the reaction is over.
hint: No more change = the reaction has stopped.

prompt: Which factor does NOT normally affect the rate of a reaction?
options: the surface area of a solid reactant
explanation: Temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts all change the rate; the container's colour does not.
hint: Three of these change collision frequency or energy — one is irrelevant.

prompt: Two reactions are run at the same concentration; one is heated, the other isn't. Which finishes first?
options: they finish at exactly the same time
explanation: Heating speeds the reaction up, so the heated one finishes sooner.
hint: Hotter = faster.

prompt: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes very slowly on its own, but adding manganese(IV) oxide makes it fizz vigorously. The manganese(IV) oxide is acting as a…
explanation: It speeds up the decomposition (2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂) without being consumed — that's a catalyst.
hint: It makes the reaction go faster but you get it all back at the end.

prompt: Increasing the pressure of a reacting GAS mixture speeds the reaction up because it…
options: squeezes the gas particles closer together, so they collide more often
explanation: Higher pressure = more particles in the same volume = more frequent collisions = faster rate (the gas-phase version of higher concentration).
hint: Pressure does to gases what concentration does to solutions.

prompt: A reaction uses marble chips and dilute acid. To make it go faster WITHOUT changing anything else, you could…
options: use the acid straight from the fridge
use the same mass of marble as a fine powder
explanation: Powdering the marble gives a much larger surface area, so the acid reacts with it faster.
hint: Same marble, smaller pieces — what does that change?

prompt: If you double the concentration of an acid reacting with magnesium, the reaction will generally…
explanation: More acid particles per unit volume → more collisions per second with the magnesium → faster reaction.
hint: More crowded particles → collisions happen more often.

prompt: Which statement about a catalyst is correct?
options: it is used up, so you need a lot of it
even a tiny amount works again and again
it makes more product than you'd get without it
explanation: Because a catalyst isn't consumed, a small amount keeps working; it changes the rate, not the amount of product.
hint: Not used up means a little goes a long way.

prompt: Why does increasing the temperature usually have a BIGGER effect on rate than increasing concentration by the same proportion?
options: it both makes collisions more frequent AND makes more collisions energetic enough to react
it removes the activation energy entirely
explanation: Concentration only makes collisions more frequent; temperature does that AND increases the fraction of collisions with enough energy — a double effect.
hint: Temperature affects two things at once; concentration affects only one.

prompt: A student measures the CO₂ given off as marble chips react with acid. The rate of reaction is fastest…
options: right at the start, when the acid is most concentrated
the rate stays constant the whole time
explanation: At the start the acid is most concentrated, so collisions are most frequent — the reaction is fastest then and slows as the acid is used up.
hint: When is the acid most concentrated — at the beginning or the end?

prompt: Two flasks contain the same mass of zinc and the same volume and concentration of acid. Flask A is at 20 °C, flask B at 40 °C. Which is true?
options: flask B reacts faster but makes the same total volume of gas
flask B makes more total gas
they react at the same rate
explanation: Heating speeds the rate up (B finishes sooner), but the amounts of zinc and acid are unchanged, so the total gas produced is the same.
hint: Hotter = faster — but the AMOUNT of product is set by how much reactant you have.

prompt: Adding a catalyst to a reaction…
options: increases the amount of product made
makes the reaction reach the same end-point sooner
explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy, so the reaction goes faster — but it produces the same amount of product, just quicker.
hint: It changes the speed, not the destination.

prompt: A reaction's rate graph rises steeply, then flattens. The flat part means…
options: all of one reactant has been used up
explanation: No more product forming = a reactant has run out = the reaction has finished.
hint: Flat line = nothing more is happening.

prompt: Surface area only affects the rate when a reactant is a…
explanation: You can only break up a solid to expose more surface; gases and liquids mix freely, so 'surface area' isn't a factor for them.
hint: Which state can you crush into smaller pieces?

prompt: Two experiments use marble + acid. Experiment 1 uses marble chips; experiment 2 uses the SAME MASS of powdered marble. Compared with experiment 1, experiment 2's rate graph will be…
options: steeper at the start and finish sooner, but reach the same final volume
steeper and make more total gas
explanation: More surface area → a faster start (steeper) and an earlier finish — but the same mass of marble, so the same total gas.
hint: Faster, but the same total amount of product.

prompt: Why is a cloud of fine flour dust (or coal dust) a serious explosion hazard?
options: fine powder has a huge surface area, so it can burn almost instantly
powder contains more atoms than lumps
explanation: A fine powder dispersed in air has an enormous surface area, so combustion can happen so fast it becomes an explosion.
hint: Think what crushing something does to its surface area — then imagine setting it alight.

prompt: Which combination would make a reaction between a solid and an acid go FASTEST?
options: large lumps of solid + cold dilute acid
large lumps of solid + hot concentrated acid
explanation: Powder (big surface area) + heat (more energetic collisions) + concentrated acid (more frequent collisions) — every factor pushes the rate up.
hint: Pick the option where every single factor speeds things up.

prompt: On a graph of 'mass of the flask' against 'time' as a gas escapes during a reaction, the rate is shown by…
options: how high the line ends up
how steeply the mass is falling at that moment
explanation: The faster the gas escapes, the faster the mass drops — so the steeper the (downward) gradient, the faster the rate.
hint: Faster reaction → mass changes more quickly → steeper slope.

prompt: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by…
options: increasing the temperature of the reactants
providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy
removing the products as they form
explanation: The catalyst offers a different route that needs less energy to get started, so a larger fraction of collisions succeed.
hint: It makes the 'energy hill' the reaction has to climb smaller.

prompt: After a reaction between magnesium and acid has finished, you recover the catalyst you added at the start. Its mass is…
options: the same as you started with
explanation: A catalyst isn't used up in the reaction, so you recover the same mass you added.
hint: Used up? No — catalysts come back unchanged.

prompt: Which change would SLOW DOWN a reaction between sodium thiosulfate solution and acid?
options: using a more concentrated thiosulfate solution
diluting the thiosulfate solution with water
explanation: Diluting lowers the concentration → fewer collisions per second → a slower reaction.
hint: Which option makes the reacting particles less crowded?

prompt: In the 'disappearing cross' experiment (a cross under a flask becomes hidden as a precipitate forms), the rate is measured by…
options: timing how long it takes for the cross to be obscured
checking the colour of the cross
explanation: The faster the precipitate forms, the sooner the cross disappears — a shorter time means a faster reaction.
hint: What are you actually timing in that experiment?

prompt: Balance the catalysed decomposition of hydrogen peroxide: __ H₂O₂ → __ H₂O + __ O₂
explanation: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ — 4 H and 4 O on each side. A catalyst like MnO₂ makes this happen fast.
hint: O₂ has 2 oxygen atoms; balance the oxygens and hydrogens — try 2 H₂O₂.

prompt: Balance the classic rate experiment: __ Mg + __ HCl → __ MgCl₂ + __ H₂
explanation: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ — 1 Mg, 2 H and 2 Cl on each side.
hint: MgCl₂ needs 2 chlorines, so you need 2 HCl — that also gives the 2 hydrogens for H₂.

prompt: An energy-profile diagram shows a reaction with and without a catalyst. The catalysed curve differs from the uncatalysed one in that it has…
explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy — the 'hump' on the diagram — so the curve peaks lower; the start and end energies (reactants and products) are unchanged.
hint: The catalyst makes the energy hill SHORTER, but the start and finish heights stay the same.

prompt: A reaction between an acid and excess marble chips produces 50 cm³ of CO₂. Repeated with the SAME acid but powdered marble, the volume of CO₂ produced will be…
explanation: Powdering changes only the rate; the amount of acid (the limiting reactant) is unchanged, so you still get 50 cm³ — just sooner.
hint: What sets the TOTAL volume — the surface area, or the amount of the limiting reactant?

prompt: Why does the rate of most reactions DECREASE as the reaction proceeds?
options: the reactant concentrations fall, so collisions become less frequent
explanation: As reactants are used up, their concentration drops, so particles collide less often — the rate slows until a reactant runs out.
hint: What happens to the amount of reactant left as time goes on?

prompt: Particle theory explains why even a small temperature rise can have a large effect on rate. The key reason is that a small rise in temperature…
options: doubles the number of particles present
greatly increases the FRACTION of particles with energy above the activation energy
changes the reactants into different substances
explanation: Only collisions with energy ≥ the activation energy react; a modest temperature rise sharply increases how many particles clear that bar (as well as making collisions more frequent).
hint: It's about how many particles can finally 'make it over the hill'.

prompt: In an experiment, doubling the concentration of one reactant roughly doubled the initial rate. This fits the idea that rate depends on…
options: how frequently the reacting particles collide
the volume of the flask only
the mass of any catalyst used
explanation: Twice the concentration → roughly twice as many collisions per second → roughly twice the initial rate.
hint: More particles in the same space → collisions happen how much more often?

prompt: Two students run the thiosulfate–acid 'disappearing cross' reaction. Student A's cross disappears in 20 s; student B's in 60 s. Which student's reaction was faster, and which probably used the more concentrated thiosulfate?
options: B was faster; B used the more concentrated solution
A was faster; A used the more concentrated solution
A was faster; B used the more concentrated solution
explanation: A shorter time = a faster reaction, so A was faster — and a more concentrated solution gives more frequent collisions, so A's was more concentrated.
hint: Less time to obscure the cross = faster; faster usually means more concentrated.

prompt: Adding a catalyst speeds up BOTH the forward and the reverse reaction in a reversible system. This tells you a catalyst changes…
options: how QUICKLY equilibrium is reached, but not where it lies
explanation: Because it lowers the activation energy equally for both directions, a catalyst reaches the same equilibrium faster — it doesn't shift it.
hint: It changes the speed of getting there, not the destination.

prompt: Iron is used as a catalyst in the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. After the process has run, the iron…
options: is recovered chemically unchanged and can be used again
explanation: Catalysts aren't consumed; the iron is recovered unchanged and reused — which is why catalysts are economically valuable.
hint: It's a catalyst — what happens to a catalyst by the end of the reaction?

prompt: Sketching a 'volume of gas vs time' graph for the same reaction at a HIGHER temperature, compared with the original, the new line should be…
options: less steep and end at a lower volume
steeper at the start and reach the same final volume sooner
steeper and end at a higher volume
explanation: Higher temperature → faster rate → a steeper line that levels off sooner — but the same amount of reactant means the same final volume.
hint: Faster start, same finishing height — just reached earlier.

prompt: Why is a reaction between two solutions usually faster than the 'same' reaction between a solid and a solution?
options: in a solution the particles are already separated and free to move and collide; in a solid only the surface particles can react
explanation: Dissolved particles can collide throughout the mixture, whereas a solid can only react where its surface is exposed.
hint: Where on a solid lump can a reaction actually happen?

prompt: A student wants to investigate how surface area affects rate. To make it a FAIR test, which must they keep the same in each run?
options: the surface area of the solid
the mass of solid, and the volume, concentration and temperature of the acid
explanation: Only the variable being tested (surface area / lump size) should change; the mass of solid and all the acid conditions must be kept constant.
hint: Change only the one thing you're testing; keep everything else fixed.

prompt: The reaction between magnesium and dilute acid is exothermic. As it runs in an insulated flask the mixture warms up. This warming…
options: has no effect on the rate
tends to raise the rate, partly offsetting the slowdown caused by the falling acid concentration
drops the rate to zero immediately
depends only on the colour of the flask
explanation: Two effects compete: falling reactant concentration slows it, but the self-heating (exothermic) tends to speed it up — the actual rate is the combination.
hint: An exothermic reaction warms its own mixture — and warmer = faster.

prompt: Balance the marble-chips-and-acid reaction: __ CaCO₃ + __ HCl → __ CaCl₂ + __ H₂O + __ CO₂
explanation: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ — 1 Ca, 1 C, 3 O, 2 H and 2 Cl on each side. The CO₂ given off is what you'd measure to find the rate.
hint: CaCl₂ needs 2 chlorines → 2 HCl; that also gives the 2 hydrogens for the water; then check the carbon and oxygen.
